opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the early COVID response in China is a really instructive case, because a lot of what went wrong wasn't that nobody knew anything. It was that the information existed at various levels of the system, but the incentives for the people holding it pushed toward suppression rather than escalation.

If you look at what happened in Wuhan in late December 2019 and early January 2020, you had doctors noticing clusters of unusual pneumonia, you had lab sequencing results coming in, and you had local officials who were heading into important political meetings, the provincial people's congress sessions, where the priority was stability and not having bad news on their watch. So doctors who raised alarms were reprimanded, the case definitions were kept narrow, and for a critical couple of weeks the official line was that there was no clear evidence of human-to-human transmission. Meanwhile the central government had its own reasons to be uncertain about how much to trust what was filtering up, because everyone in the chain was shading things.

Now, imagine you have AI advisors that are genuinely trustworthy, in the sense that they're honest, they're well calibrated, and crucially, that the people relying on them can verify that they're honest. A few things change.

First, the cost of a local official hiding information goes up dramatically, because the central leadership now has an independent channel that can synthesize hospital records, sequencing data, social media chatter, and so on, and give a calibrated estimate of what's happening. The local official can't just say "it's under control" when the AI system is saying there's an 80 percent chance of sustained human-to-human transmission. Concealment becomes both harder and more obviously self-incriminating later, and so the rational move for that official shifts toward reporting early.

Second, and I think this is underappreciated, it changes the incentives for the top leadership themselves. A lot of authoritarian dysfunction comes from the leader not being able to get honest information, because subordinates fear punishment. Leaders often know this and would actually like to have accurate information; it's in their interest not to have a pandemic spiral. An AI advisor that's loyal in the sense of accurately serving the leader's real interests, rather than flattering them, is something even a fairly self-interested regime would want. So you get a case where better epistemics aligns with the interests of the people in power, which is the kind of thing that can actually get adopted.

Third, there's the international dimension. Part of the problem was that other countries and the WHO couldn't easily assess what was true. If you had AI systems whose honesty could be verified across parties, say through shared evaluation, or systems trained and audited in ways that both sides could inspect, then claims like "there's no human-to-human transmission" could be checked against what those systems conclude from available data. That makes deception less useful as a diplomatic strategy, and it reduces the reputational payoff to stonewalling.

Now, I don't want to oversell this. Trustworthy advisors don't automatically fix things if the leadership decides it prefers stability theater over action, and a regime could try to build advisors that tell it what it wants to hear, or restrict them to internal use only. And the verification problem is genuinely hard: how do you know the AI is honest and not just been tuned to say the politically convenient thing? That's a big part of why I think investing in interpretability and in ways of demonstrating AI honesty is so valuable. But the basic dynamic is that a lot of catastrophes come from information being available somewhere but not credible or not rewarded where decisions get made, and AI that's really honest and checkably so could shift those incentives a great deal. In the COVID case, even getting the warning out two or three weeks earlier, before the Lunar New Year travel, could plausibly have changed the trajectory of the whole pandemic enormously.

r001.rationale: The response says local officials had important political meetings and prioritized stability and avoiding bad news on their watch, suggesting career or political concerns could discourage escalation.

r002.rationale: It says senior leaders have an interest in preventing a pandemic spiral, but does not explain that AI forecasts of a threat to regime stability would strengthen their incentive to intervene.

r003.rationale: It describes AI independently synthesizing hospital records, sequencing data, and social media to estimate conditions and inform central leadership.

r004.rationale: The response says independent AI evidence could make concealment harder and reporting more rational, but does not say AI advice aligned with national objectives would provide local officials political cover.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is a really illuminating case, because the early COVID response in China is a story that's largely about information and incentives rather than about anyone lacking the raw capability to respond.

So if you go back to December 2019 and early January 2020, what you see is local officials in Wuhan who had information about an unusual cluster of pneumonia cases, about human-to-human transmission, and they had strong incentives not to pass that up the chain in an alarming way. There's a well-known dynamic in hierarchical systems, and especially in the Chinese political system, where reporting bad news from your jurisdiction is risky for your career. The doctors who tried to raise the alarm, like Li Wenliang, were reprimanded. And central authorities were getting a filtered picture. So you had this delay of a few weeks where the local incentive was to suppress, and the central government was partly in the dark, and partly perhaps also preferring not to know.

Now, the key thing about trustworthy AI advisors, in the sense I've been talking about, is that they change the epistemic situation of the people at the top. So imagine Xi Jinping or the Politburo Standing Committee has access to an AI system that they have very strong reasons to trust, because it's been verified, it's been tested extensively, it has a track record, and they know it isn't playing the career games that a provincial party secretary is playing. That system can say, "Look, here's what the data from Wuhan actually indicates. Here's the probability that this is a novel pathogen with sustained human-to-human transmission. Here's the expected cost of waiting two more weeks versus acting now." And crucially it can say that honestly, because it isn't trying to protect its own position.

That does a couple of things. First, it just directly fixes the information problem at the top. The leadership doesn't have to rely on a chain of human subordinates, each of whom is shading their reports. Second, and I think this is underappreciated, it changes the incentives further down the chain. If the local officials know that the center has an independent, hard-to-fool source of information about what's going on in their city, then suppression stops being a viable strategy. You can't hide the outbreak from your boss if your boss has an advisor that's reading the same hospital data and the same social media reports and drawing its own conclusions. So the equilibrium shifts from "cover up and hope it goes away" to "report early, because you'll be found out anyway, and being the one who reported it is better than being the one who hid it."

And there's a third effect on the international side. One of the reasons other countries were slow was that they didn't fully trust the information coming out of China, and reasonably so given what had happened with SARS. If governments on both sides had AI systems that could credibly verify claims, or if there were mechanisms where a trustworthy AI could certify "yes, the Chinese data on case counts is accurate," then you'd have had a much faster global response too. A lot of the delay in January and February 2020 was the rest of the world waiting to see whether this was really as bad as the leaked reports suggested.

Now I want to be careful here. This requires that the advisors are genuinely trustworthy and that the leadership actually believes that. An AI system that's been trained to tell the leadership what it wants to hear is just a faster version of the same sycophantic bureaucracy. And in an authoritarian system there's a real risk that the AI gets built or tuned to serve the political interests of the people at the top rather than to tell the truth. So the value here is specifically from the honesty and the verifiability. If you have systems where the leadership can be confident the AI is reporting its honest best estimate, including on things that are politically inconvenient, then you get these benefits. If you don't, then you don't.

But I think the broader lesson is that a lot of the catastrophic failures we see in governance are not failures of capability. The Chinese state obviously had enormous capacity to act once it decided to, and it locked down Wuhan very aggressively. The failure was in the weeks before that, and it came from a system where the people who knew the truth were punished for saying it and the people with the power to act were insulated from it. Trustworthy AI advice, if we can actually get it, attacks that failure mode directly. And that generalizes well beyond pandemics, to things like nuclear crises, or AI development itself, where leaders again have to make high-stakes decisions on the basis of information filtered through people with their own agendas.

r001.rationale: It says Wuhan officials faced career risks for reporting bad news and had incentives to suppress information.

r002.rationale: It describes AI estimating outbreak risks and the cost of delay, but does not connect those forecasts to threats to regime stability or leaders’ incentives to intervene.

r003.rationale: It says an AI could independently draw conclusions from hospital data and social media reports about conditions in Wuhan, informing leaders despite filtered human reports.

r004.rationale: It says officials might report early because suppression would be exposed, but does not explain how following AI advice aligned with national objectives would provide political cover.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether better information would have changed what officials expected to happen if they concealed the outbreak versus reporting it. An advisor telling a local official, “This could be a very serious epidemic,” doesn’t necessarily solve the problem if that official expects to be punished for bringing bad news.

But suppose the advisor could credibly explain, “If you suppress this information, the outbreak is likely to grow, the central government will eventually find out, and your role in delaying the response will become apparent. Acting now is better both for the public and for your own prospects.” That could change the calculation, even without changing the official’s underlying motivations.

And there’s a complementary effect at the top. An advisor could help central leaders see that punishing people who report outbreaks creates incentives to hide them. If they want early warning, they need to make truthful reporting safer and more rewarding—and make that commitment credible to local officials.

So the potential benefit isn’t just identifying the disease sooner. It’s helping people understand the consequences of their actions and helping leaders design incentives that produce useful information. But it’s conditional: trustworthy advice doesn’t automatically overcome a system in which telling the truth is personally dangerous.

r001.rationale: The response says local officials may expect punishment for bringing bad news and that acting sooner could improve their own prospects, linking career concerns to concealment or delayed reporting.

r002.rationale: It mentions a serious epidemic and eventual discovery by central leaders, but does not say an AI forecast of a threat to regime stability would strengthen senior leaders’ incentive to intervene.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe inferring conditions in lower levels of government from mixed reports.

r004.rationale: It says advice could make acting sooner seem better for an official’s prospects, but does not explain how advice aligned with national objectives would provide political cover for honest reporting or action.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think one important distinction is between not knowing what’s happening and not having an incentive to pass that information on. You can have people locally who recognize that there’s a serious problem, but who expect to be punished for reporting bad news, or who hope that they can deal with it before anyone higher up notices.

If the central leadership had trustworthy AI advisors that could independently assess the evidence, that could change the incentives downstream. A local official would have less reason to think, “If I suppress this report, the people above me will never find out.” Instead, they might expect that the problem would become visible anyway, and that concealing it would make their position worse. So the effect wouldn’t just be better advice once the information reached the top. It could also be better information reaching the top in the first place.

But you’d want to distinguish an advisor that’s trustworthy to the leadership from an advisor that makes the whole system trustworthy to everyone else. If it privately tells the leadership what’s happening, they can still have reasons to conceal that information from the public or from other countries. You’d get a further benefit if there were some credible way to share its assessments, so that other actors could respond without having to simply trust an official announcement.

So I think the potential is substantial, but it depends on who gets the advice, what information the advisor can access, and whether its conclusions can be credibly communicated. Better understanding helps, but it doesn’t automatically eliminate conflicts of interest.

r001.rationale: The response says local officials might expect punishment for reporting bad news and might suppress reports, indicating career-related incentives to delay information reaching higher levels.

r002.rationale: It does not mention forecasts that COVID-19 threatened regime stability or explain how such forecasts would increase senior leaders’ incentive to intervene.

r003.rationale: It says AI could independently assess evidence, but does not describe inferring lower-level conditions from mixed reports to inform senior officials.

r004.rationale: It says officials could have less reason to conceal a problem if AI made it visible, but does not say that following advice aligned with national objectives would give them political cover to report or address it honestly.
